# Localisation beyond translation

Google's internationalisation talk treated localisation as more than translation: machine translation may be acceptable, at the site owner's judgement, after weighing translation quality, local conventions such as date formats and calendars (in Thailand the current year, as of 2026, is 2569) and cultural adaptation, and Google's spam policies list automated translation of scraped content as an example of scaled content abuse. Consumer data shown in the talk (source not captured) suggested that trust cues differ by market: promotions and discounts matter to shoppers in Europe and the US, reviews weigh more in the US, brand reputation in Europe, expert recommendations and certifications in Germany, and product origin in France (said at the event, not in Google's docs). The talk also warned that AI answers are still language-dependent: if an answer is synthesised from the top results, a query in another language draws on different data, so missing or weak local content becomes an invisible gap that site owners should check per language and market. John Mueller explained that the notranslate rule opts a page out of Google Search's translation features (documented) and that its form in a meta tag named google also turns off Chrome's automatic translation (said at the event; a 2008 Search Central blog post says that form stops Google Translate, and Chromium's Translate design document says it disables Chrome's translation), adding that he dislikes the rule because translation is a form of accessibility. A community speaker argued that understanding each market is harder than hreflang, citing an audit in which a correctly translated Dutch site converted far worse than its sister sites because the region had never been checked (Dutch homes are narrow, on several floors, with steep stairs), and noting that regional demand shifts over time, as a chart of search interest in ceiling fans in northern versus southern Europe showed. Day 3 added that Google does not prefer English words on pages in other languages, and that where it recognises an English term and its local equivalent as synonyms a page needs only one of them; Google called a gap in results for a language an opportunity for whoever targets those words, and repeated that some countries rely heavily on reviews as social proof (said at the event). A second recording of Day 2 added that working out a site's localized pages and which countries it targets is one of the difficult, complex tasks for Google in indexing, and the non-Latin-script talk saw AI answers to Persian queries written in Persian but citing English sources where Persian content was thin, concluding that multilingual SEO is more than translation: script, typing habits and market maturity must be fitted to each market. On Day 1 a community speaker showed that AI fan-out queries are often in another language than the prompt, citing a study heard as Peec AI's and a Spanish prompt about Barcelona restaurants that fanned out in English. Author's view: Peec AI's published study found English fan-outs in nearly 78% of non-English prompt runs, from 66% for Spanish to 94% for Turkish, and 43% of the fan-out searches for those prompts ran in English.

Based on: `D2-C608`, `D2-C610`, `D2-C611`, `D2-C613`, `D2-C614`, `D2-C615`, `D2-C616`, `D2-C603`, `D2-C602`, `D2-C606`, `D2-C093`, `D2-C095`, `D2-C094`, `D2-C096`, `D2-C097`, `D2-C634`, `D2-C619`, `D2-C623`, `D2-C624`, `D2-C635`, `D2-C636`, `D3-C041`, `D3-C042`, `D3-C081`, `D3-C341`, `D2-C961`, `D2-C972`, `D2-C973`, `D2-C966`, `D1-C295`, `D1-C294`, `D1-C504`.

## What to do

- Treat machine translation as a first draft: have native speakers review it and adapt dates, calendars, units and regional vocabulary before publishing, because bulk translation that adds little value can fall under scaled content abuse.
- Check AI Overviews and AI Mode with native-language queries in each market and compare with the country breakdown of the Generative AI performance report.
- Localise product range, photography, pricing, payment options and trust signals per market, and test the order of reviews, brand, certifications and origin information.
- Remove notranslate from templates unless translation must be prevented.
- Re-check regional demand at least yearly in Google Trends for the exact country or region before localising for a market.
- Write pages in the local language without adding English terms for Google's sake; add the other term only where readers need it.

## What Google's documentation says

- **[Docs]** Google's Search documentation gives notranslate as a rule for a robots or googlebot meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag header, and says the rule opts a page out of all translation features in Google Search.
  <br><sub>`D2-C095` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing · is the documentation · [Translated results in Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/translated-results), [Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag) · Used by `DEV-IDX-03`, `DEV-IDX-09`, the glossary term *X-Robots-Tag*</sub>

- **[Docs]** A 2008 Search Central blog post says a meta tag named google with the value notranslate stops Google Translate from translating any of a page's content.
  <br><sub>`D2-C096` · Search Central blog (14 October 2008) · annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing · is the documentation · [Helping you break the language barrier](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2008/10/helping-you-break-language-barrier) · Used by `DEV-IDX-09`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's Search Help says the language a query is typed in is an important factor in choosing the language of results, alongside interface and device language, location and site owners' annotations, and that Google may also show results in other languages when they are helpful or when there is not enough information in the query's language.
  <br><sub>`D2-C604` · Google Search Help · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · is the documentation · [How Google knows what language to show in search results](https://support.google.com/websearch/answer/13511324?hl=en)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's spam policies define scaled content abuse as generating many pages mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value to users, no matter how they are created, and list automated translating of scraped content among the examples.
  <br><sub>`D2-C611` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · is the documentation · [Spam policies for Google web search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) · Extended by [D3-C695](../sessions/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) · Extended by [D3-C697](../sessions/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) · Used by `DEV-INT-10`, the glossary term *Scaled content abuse*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's documentation recommends hreflang annotations even when a site's versions differ only by small regional variations within one language, for example English-language content targeted to the US, GB and Ireland.
  <br><sub>`D2-C628` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation · is the documentation · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-08`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's documentation lists the signals it uses to decide which locale a page targets: ccTLDs, hreflang statements, server location, and other signals such as local addresses and phone numbers, local language and currency, links from other local sites and Business Profile signals.
  <br><sub>`D2-C632` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation · is the documentation · [Managing multi-regional and multilingual sites](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/managing-multi-regional-sites) · Used by `DEV-INT-08`</sub>

## Analysis

- **[Analysis]** The study cited on stage matches Peec AI's analysis (reported in February 2026) of over 10 million ChatGPT prompts and 20 million fan-outs: 43% of the fan-out searches for non-English prompts ran in English, and nearly 78% of non-English prompt runs had at least one English fan-out (from 66% for Spanish to 94% for Turkish), so the 43% is a share of fan-out searches, not of prompts.
  <br><sub>`D1-C504` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI · [ChatGPT searches in English, even when you don't](https://peec.ai/blog/chatgpt-searches-in-english-even-when-you-don-t), [ChatGPT Search Often Switches To English In Fan-Out Queries: Report](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/chatgpt-search-often-switches-to-english-in-fan-out-queries-report/567811/) · Extends [D1-C294](../sessions/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** International sites should remove notranslate from their templates unless translation must be prevented: the robots or googlebot form switches off Google Search's translation features, and John Mueller said the form named google also blocks Chrome's translation for visitors who do not read the language.
  <br><sub>`D2-C098` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing · Used by `DEV-IDX-09`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** For German-language sites serving Germany, Austria and Switzerland, add hreflang with region codes (de-DE, de-AT, de-CH) and make the country pages differ in more than boilerplate (prices, shipping, legal details), or expect Google to cluster them and show one.
  <br><sub>`D2-C384` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Handling web duplication · Used by `DEV-INT-08`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Check AI Overviews and AI Mode with native-language queries in each target market, not with translated English keywords, and compare with the country breakdown of Search Console's generative AI performance report; topics where competitors are cited and you are not point to missing or weak local content.
  <br><sub>`D2-C607` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · [Introducing Search Generative AI performance reports in Search Console](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/06/gen-ai-performance-reports) · Extends [D1-C124](../sessions/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-07`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Treat machine translation as a first draft: have a native speaker review it and adapt dates, calendars and units before publishing, because unreviewed bulk translation that adds little value can also fall under Google's scaled content abuse policy.
  <br><sub>`D2-C612` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · Extends [D1-C048](../sessions/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by `DEV-INT-10`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Localise the trust signals on product pages, not only the words: if the findings shown hold for your category, lead with reviews in the US, brand reputation elsewhere in Europe, expert certifications in Germany and origin information in France, and test the order per market.
  <br><sub>`D2-C617` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation</sub>

- **[Analysis]** When translations and hreflang are clean but one country version converts far worse, compare that market's product range, photography and delivery or installation constraints with local competitors before changing anything technical.
  <br><sub>`D2-C625` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Re-check regional demand for core product categories at least once a year, for example by comparing regions and seasons in Google Trends, because climate, housing or habits can shift what a market wants.
  <br><sub>`D2-C637` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Treat hreflang as a way to show the right language version, not as a market-entry signal: before launching a country version, make sure local publications, partners or directories already mention the brand, and localise pricing and payment options.
  <br><sub>`D2-C641` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation</sub>

- **[Analysis]** List language variants such as fr-FR and fr-BE or de-DE and de-CH separately in a site's language inventory, and give each its own vocabulary and spelling review instead of reusing one translation for every country.
  <br><sub>`D2-C642` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation</sub>

- **[Analysis]** For Persian and Arabic keyword research, look up each lookalike-character spelling of a term separately and add up the volumes, and check which variant the site's own content uses.
  <br><sub>`D2-C647` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The lower selection bar in under-served languages is an opening for content written for that market, not for machine translation at scale: index selection also applies spam signals, and Google's spam policies count generating many pages from scraped content through automated transformations such as translating, with little value for users, as scaled content abuse.
  <br><sub>`D2-C692` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? · [Spam policies for Google web search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) · Used by `DEV-INT-10`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Compare candidate keywords in Google Trends for the exact country or region where the page should rank, because the higher-interest wording can differ between markets that share a language.
  <br><sub>`D2-C793` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Google Trends</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The regional search interest maps in Google Trends give a quick first check of demand by country or region before localising content for a new market.
  <br><sub>`D2-C817` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Google Trends</sub>

## Built on these claims

The items of the developer and content kits that rest on this topic's claims.

- Requirement `DEV-IDX-03`: Send robots rules for PDFs, images and other non-HTML files in the X-Robots-Tag header
- Requirement `DEV-IDX-09`: Leave notranslate and noimageindex out of templates unless translation or image indexing must be prevented
- Requirement `DEV-INT-07`: Make each page's language unambiguous by translating the template with the main content
- Requirement `DEV-INT-08`: Differentiate same-language country versions beyond boilerplate and mark them with region codes
- Requirement `DEV-INT-10`: Publish machine-translated language versions only after human review and localisation
- Requirement `DEV-INT-11`: Write pages in the words, spellings and script the audience searches with, and never add synonym or variant lists
- Requirement `DEV-INT-12`: Mark the text direction of right-to-left and mixed-script titles, product names and URLs
- Requirement `DEV-MON-07`: Track AI feature visibility in the Generative AI performance report
- Requirement `DEV-SDA-05`: Write dates in ISO 8601 and give every date-time a UTC offset
- Glossary term *Bidirectional text*
- Glossary term *Scaled content abuse*
- Glossary term *X-Robots-Tag*
